title: Startup identity and the sadness of a successful exit: why founders feel loss after selling
summary: Jason Cohen explains why nearly every founder feels deep sadness after selling, even after a big win: the startup is the founder's identity, not a job. He argues selling can still be right, and that founders should decide based on the CEO role they want as the company matures, not on money.

principles.text: A startup is the founder's identity, not a job, which is why selling it feels like losing yourself.
principles.quote: A startup is an obsession. You do it because you couldn't stop yourself. Because when you were doing anything else, you were thinking about it.

principles.text: Painful does not mean wrong: sell when it's the right call, even if you love the company.
principles.quote: Just because it's painful doesn't mean you don't need to do it.

principles.text: Don't expect a big payout to make you fulfilled or happy; build fulfillment independent of the exit.
principles.quote: You must resist the urge to believe that getting millions of dollars will make you fulfilled, or happy.

principles.text: The CEO job changes as the company grows, whether or not you sell, so check you want the later-stage role.
principles.quote: The CEO's job description changes over time, and so does the company, whether you sell it or not. Are you emotionally prepared for this as well?

principles.text: Successful startups mature into process-heavy businesses; founders must be ready to give up hands-on control.
principles.quote: The fact is, successful startups grow up. They grow into businesses and mature into sustainability, risk-avoidance, HR law, strategic planning, executive meetings, and all that.

principles.text: Time the exit to the role you want: Cohen sold before needing to manage managers, once the payout crossed the Freedom Line.
principles.quote: So for me I sold at a good point: before I needed a C_O, but after the company was big enough to garner enough money to cross the Freedom Line.
